claims.claim: Ruth Graves Wakefield (1903-1977) studied home economics and was a dietitian and lecturer.

evidence.quote: Ruth Graves Wakefield (1903-1977) studied home economics and was a dietician and lecturer.

claims.claim: In 1930 she opened the Toll House Inn with her husband Kenneth in Whitman, Massachusetts, south of Boston, and ran it with him.

evidence.quote: In 1930, she opened the Toll House Inn, with her husband Kenneth, in Whitman, Massachusetts, south of Boston.
the Toll House Inn in Whitman, MA, which she ran with her husband

claims.claim: The cookie was an accident: Wakefield ran out of nuts, or of cocoa/baking chocolate, chopped up a chocolate bar and expected the pieces to melt into a chocolate cookie, but they did not.

evidence.quote: There are a couple of origin stories for the chocolate chip cookie that promote the idea that the invention was an accident.
evidence.location: 'origin stories' paragraph; variants: 'Ruth ran out of nuts…' and 'Ruth ran out of cocoa…'

evidence.quote: thinking they would melt and she'd have her chocolate cookies. But, much to her surprise, the pieces did not melt

claims.limits: The narration tells the cocoa/baking-chocolate variant and labels it 'the story goes'.

claims.claim: In the 1970s Wakefield dismissed the 'accidental' origin stories; she said adding the chocolate pieces to the batter was intentional.

evidence.quote: in the 1970s, Ruth dismissed the 'accidental' origin stories
adding them to a batter was intentional and not an accident.
evidence.location: same paragraph, crediting Nick O'Malley, MassLive, Oct. 31, 2024

claims.limits: Second-hand: the Library of Congress relays a reporter's finding; the 1970s interview itself was not read. Narration attributes it to her ('she said') and the hook says 'probably'.

claims.claim: The recipe appeared in Wakefield's 1938 cookbook 'Toll House Tried and True Recipes' (M. Barrows and Company), p. 165, first named the 'Chocolate Crunch Cookie', later the 'Toll House Chocolate Crunch Cookie'.

evidence.quote: Ruth Wakefield's 1938 'Toll House Tried and True Recipes' (New York, M. Barrows and Company)
The cookie was originally called the 'Chocolate Crunch Cookie' and later the 'Toll House Chocolate Crunch Cookie.'
The cookie first appeared on p. 165 in this edition.

claims.limits: When she first baked it (1930s, before 1938) is not dated in the sources read; narration only says the cookbook year.

claims.claim: In 1939 Nestlé asked Wakefield to feature her recipe on its chocolate bars (the 2010 post adds: in return for a lifetime supply of chocolate).

evidence.quote: in 1939, Nestle asked Ruth if they could feature her recipe on their bars of chocolate.
they offered to print the Toll House Cookie recipe on the bars in return for giving Ruth a life-time supply.

claims.limits: Narration says 'a year later, a chocolate company asked to print her recipe on its bars'; the lifetime-supply detail is not used.

claims.claim: The original recipe told bakers to chop chocolate bars into pea-sized pieces; chocolate chips were not yet sold.

evidence.quote: The original 'Toll House Chocolate Crunch Cookie' recipe instructed bakers to chop up bars of chocolate into pea-sized pieces
2 bars (7 oz) Nestles yellow label chocolate, semi-sweet, which has been cut in pieces the size of a pea.

claims.claim: Nestlé then began selling chocolate already shaped into small pieces (morsels) to save bakers the chopping: 1939 per the 2010 post, 'by 1940' per the 2025 post.

evidence.quote: By 1940, however, Nestle introduced bars of chocolate molded into tiny square pieces
In 1939, Nestles created the morsels to save us from chopping up the bars.

claims.limits: Year differs between the two posts (1939 vs by 1940), so no year is spoken. The 2025 wording describes bars molded into small squares, the 2010 wording 'morsels'; narration says 'chocolate already made in tiny pieces', which fits both.

claims.claim: Wakefield sold the Toll House name to Nestlé for $1 plus free chocolate for life.

evidence.quote: in return for giving Ruth a life-time supply.

claims.limits: Neither Library of Congress post mentions $1; only the lifetime supply appears in the 2010 post. NOT used.

claims.claim: Massachusetts made the chocolate chip cookie its official state cookie in 1997.
claims.limits: Only seen in search results; the law page could not be opened. NOT used in the Short.
